speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: asked	the Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) (a) whether current retail petrol prices at petrol pumps reflect the fall in oil prices; (b) whether there is a trend of petrol companies increasing prices faster than they decrease when there are changes to the oil prices; and (c) if so, whether the Ministry plans to implement measures to ensure that petrol companies adjust prices accordingly.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: asked	the Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) whether the Competition Commission of Singapore regularly monitors the price of petrol in Singapore to ensure that there are no cartel practices that will breach the competition rules in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: asked	the Minister for Trade and Industry (Industry) in view of local petrol prices not falling as much as crude oil prices, whether the Competition Commission of Singapore will consider launching an inquiry on the practices of local oil companies.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In 2015, the Competition Commission of Singapore (CCS) commenced a study on the factors affecting the movement of petrol prices in Singapore since 2010.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Crude oil price is the price of unrefined oil while MOPS price is the price at which petrol companies purchase refined wholesale petrol from the refineries.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: MOPS price tends to be higher than crude oil price as it includes the cost of refining crude oil into wholesale petrol.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In 2015, MOPS price made up less than one-third of the listed retail petrol price.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Other components of retail petrol price include operating costs, taxes and duties, land costs, discounts and rebates.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: These non-fuel components have generally increased in the past few years.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The retail petrol price that consumers generally pay includes the petrol levy as well as discounts and rebates.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Consumers enjoyed an average of about 18% in discounts and rebates off the listed price for Octane 95 petrol in 2014 through site discounts, loyalty programmes and credit card payment.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The pass-through, while relatively high at around 70%, is not complete because of the non-fuel components which make up more than two-thirds of listed retail petrol price.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Over the six-year period between 1 January 2010 and 31 January 2016, CCS observed that the listed prices for Octane 95 petrol moved in tandem with MOPS prices.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: There was no significant variation between the time taken to either raise or lower the listed prices for Octane 95 petrol in response to changes in MOPS prices.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The magnitude of the change in listed prices for Octane 95 	Page: 9 petrol relative to the change of MOPS prices was also observed to be the same, whether MOPS prices increased or decreased.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: CCS will continue to monitor developments in the retail petrol market.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We are not saying that they are colluding but we are not happy with the amount of the reduction in the petrol price.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The next question: could it be that there is a lack of competition in Singapore as there are just a few of them?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Ministry consider removing the three-quarter tank rule?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The smaller percentage drop largely reflects the fact that MOPS price made up only a third of the listed retail price.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, a third of S$0.52 would be a ballpark of about 15%.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The lack of complete pass-through could also be due to changes in non-fuel components, as I have listed earlier.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As to whether we will be studying this further, yes, CCS will continue to monitor and study.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We will be embarking on a study on the supply side of the equation to see if consumer behaviour does affect pricing from the petrol companies.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: CCS said that MOPS price makes up about one third of the listed retail petrol price.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: When we look at the average MOPS price of Octane 95 last week, it was about US$46.5 per barrel.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Three times of that average MOPS price is about US$139.5 per barrel.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: When we look at the retail price of Octane 95 in Singapore at the petrol kiosks, it costs about S$1.82 per litre before discount.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Even if we are given a discount of 15% on average, it costs about S$1.55 per litre or US$174.64 per barrel, as compared to three times the MOPS price which is equivalent to US$139.5 per barrel.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: That is, the retail price of Octane 95 is US$35.14 higher than US$139.50, or 25% more.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It appears that the petrol companies are charging Singaporeans at least 25% more.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: A lot of Singaporeans are looking towards the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) to help us to regulate retail petrol prices, so that we are not over-charged.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I hope the Minister of State can look into it.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Listed prices are prices that are observed at petrol stations, for example, those that are displayed at the pumps.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Effective prices are listed prices that exclude the levy hike introduced in February 2015, but have factored in the discounts and the rebates that are enjoyed by the consumers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The price that 	Page: 10 consumers pay will be the listed prices minus the discounts and the rebates.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Unfortunately, CCS is unable to provide further details about the change in the operating income at the company level, as such information is deemed to be commercially sensitive.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As to whether the companies are profiteering, on average, the operating income of petrol companies has generally increased over the past years.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As I have said earlier, this increase is smaller relative to the increase in the non-fuel components, such as operating costs, taxes and duties, land cost, discounts and rebates.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: An increase in profit, in itself, is not a contravention of the Competition Act, unless the increase is due to market players engaging in anti-competitive behaviours, which would contravene the Competition Act.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Based on information that CCS has gathered in the market study, there is no evidence to suggest whether there is any collusion in petrol pricing even though they do monitor the prices.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Consumers, generally, as the Member pointed out, do enjoy discounts and rebates off the petrol prices.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The discounts and rebates, especially for credit cards, are quite variable and are not easily comparable due to varying terms and conditions.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Consumer Association of Singapore (CASE) did a study recently and realised that despite crude oil prices coming down, the price of Octane 98 went up by S$0.02.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The other question that I wish to ask the Minister of State is whether MTI would consider encouraging a third party, for example, the cooperatives under the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC), to run another petrol company, so that we would have greater competition.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is very much like what the Infocomm Development Authority of Singapore (IDA) did to introduce a fourth telco to provide greater competition, so that our consumers have greater choices.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: There is currently no legal requirement for petrol companies to display their pump prices prominently.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: CCS notes that the reason why petrol companies do not display their prices prominently is because, in certain jurisdictions overseas, petrol companies are accused of anti-competitive price signalling when they do so, when it is not legally required to do so in the first place.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That said, CCS recognises that improved price transparency in the retail petrol market may facilitate easier comparison and more informed petrol buying decisions by consumers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As to whether we should be having another petrol player in the market, that will be a commercial decision that NTUC has to take.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I am not sure whether NTUC is contemplating this in the first place.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The petrol companies do make a profit but as long as the profit that they make is not in excess of what is a reasonable margin that other similar petrol companies make over the same time period, I do not think that they are making a profit at the expense of consumers.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Mr Low, do you have a follow-up question?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: How does the Minister of State know that the profit made by the petrol companies is not excessive and, if so, by what standard?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: MOPS pricing was also used as an international standard in pricing for petrol sale across jurisdictions, so I think that is a fair method for pricing crude oil and how retail petrol is being used in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One is to regulate more and look more closely.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second is actually to open up competition.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One way of doing this will be, as the Minister of State had mentioned, to have more price transparency.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In doing that, I would also suggest that any discounts and so on be factored in; otherwise, it is very difficult for customers to track what a 10% or 15% discount on this price is.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: MOPS prices are also used in the region as a price benchmark to make an assessment of the financial value of oils which are transferred from upstream production to refineries and, subsequently, to the market.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, in terms of pricing of petrol, how the price varies with crude oil 	Page: 12 changes, I think that has been used as a consistent and fair international benchmark.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: As to whether we should continue to open up competition, as suggested by the Member, I think that is something that we will continue to study and see if the market is suitable for such an introduction.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: I think the Minister of State has not answered both my questions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: I asked if the Ministry studied the price of petrol during the last cycle of the upward trend of crude oil.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: What he explained on MOPS pricing, we do not understand, but perhaps we could take a look at the upward trend of crude oil prices in the last round and how fast the petrol companies increased their pump prices.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: The other question is on removing the three-quarter tank rule so that there is more competition.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, on a day-to-day basis, the level of pass-through and time taken for adjustments may deviate due to fluctuations in the fuel and non-fuel components but, on the whole, the fluctuations do reflect the changes in the petrol pricing.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: On the three-quarter tank rule, that is something we have to continue to study and see the merits of whether it is something we should implement.
